title: Chimera: A Hybrid GPU Backend for Sumcheck Acceleration in Zero Knowledge Provers
authors: Kashfia Farheen and Nektarios Georgios Tsoutsos
abstract:
Zero-knowledge proof systems are increasingly relying on the Sumcheck protocol to avoid the FFT-heavy structure of earlier SNARK designs. Sumcheck is well suited for GPU acceleration; it consists of sequential rounds where each round performs regular, parallelizable operations over large multilinear evaluation tables. The focus is on how to organize this work across rounds: intuitively, the active polynomial state should remain close to the device that processes it, the CPU-GPU boundary should only expose values that are needed to transition, and various cryptographic settings should be kept stable.

This paper presents Chimera, a GPU-CPU framework for accelerating Sumcheck in Spartan-style SNARK provers. Chimera uses a hybrid execution model: large polynomial evaluation and folding work runs on the GPU, active polynomial state remains resident on GPU across profitable rounds, compact round messages return to Spartan's host transcript, and small domains fall back to CPU execution. Chimera also specializes the wrappers around Spartan's small round-polynomial commitments and proof objects, and introduces a memory-aware chunking path.


On BN254 Spartan R1CS instances, Chimera demonstrates a \(7.96\times\) improvement of the committed-Sumcheck region at \(N=2^{17}\),  relative to clean Spartan. Across full Spartan proving runs from \(2^{12}\) to \(2^{27}\) constraints, Chimera improves end-to-end prover time for all measured sizes, reaching \(1.27\times\)-\(1.64\times\) speedup for sizes \(2^{24}\)-\(2^{27}\). Ablation studies show that Chimera's gains come from choosing the right execution boundary rather than from any single optimization. The GPU handles the large, regular Sumcheck work, while Spartan keeps the protocol state needed for transcript and verifier compatibility. This reduces movement of polynomial data without disrupting the proof system. The remaining gap between Sumcheck-region and end-to-end speedup shows that, after Sumcheck is accelerated, polynomial commitment and proof-wrapper costs become the next bottleneck.

      compact round messages return to Spartan’s host transcript, and small domains fall back to CPU exe-

      Sumcheck region at N = 217 , relative to clean Spartan. Across full Spartan proving runs from 212 to
      227 constraints, Chimera improves end-to-end prover time for all measured sizes, reaching 1.27×–1.64×

      Keywords: Zero-knowledge proofs · Sumcheck · GPU acceleration.


1   Introduction
Zero-knowledge proofs allow a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true without revealing the
private data used to prove it [7]. In modern zkSNARK systems, the proof is compact and verification is
fast, but proof generation remains computationally expensive and slow [6,8,15]. This prover cost is the main
barrier for practical deployments such as private payments, blockchain scalability, verifiable outsourcing,
privacy-preserving analytics, and zkML [5, 10, 13, 17, 21]. In such applications, the prover must process large
constraint systems and execute expensive operations, so reducing prover latency has become a core systems
problem involving arithmetic throughput, memory movement, scheduling, and protocol integration.
    Prior ZKP acceleration work has attacked the prover bottleneck with distributed systems, GPUs, FPGAs,
ASICs, and programmable accelerators. Systems such as DIZK, cuZK, GZKP, PipeZK, BatchZK, PipeMSM,
SZKP, NoCap, UniZK, zkSpeed, and zkPHIRE show that prover latency depends on arithmetic throughput,
memory movement, batching, scheduling, and hardware/software co-design [2–4, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16–18, 21].
Much of this work focuses on kernels that dominate transform- or commitment-heavy provers, such as MSM,
NTT/FFT, polynomial evaluation, and finite-field arithmetic. At the same time, several recent prover systems
are increasingly using multilinear polynomial representations and Sumcheck-based arguments to obtain linear
time or near-linear time prover structure [1,12,15,19,20]. This shifts an important part of the prover work from
large transform stages to round-based arithmetic over multilinear evaluation tables. Sumcheck repeatedly
scans large evaluation tables, reduces them to compact round messages, derives challenges, and folds the
active state for the next round. Each round exposes abundant parallelism, but the rounds are connected by
Fiat-Shamir challenges. This makes Sumcheck acceleration sensitive not only to field-arithmetic speed, but
also to memory residency, launch overhead, synchronization, and round-to-round data movement.
    A single Sumcheck round kernel on GPU is therefore not sufficient for accelerating a full prover. In
Spartan, Sumcheck is embedded inside a committed proof system [15]. The prover must preserve a fixed
transcript schedule, commit to small round-polynomial objects, update target commitments, construct dot-
product proofs, and assemble verifier-compatible proof objects. Moving only the round evaluation arithmetic
to the GPU leaves much of this surrounding work on the critical path. Conversely, moving the entire protocol
to the GPU would conflict with Spartan’s host-visible transcript and proof interface, and sometimes lead to
slowdown of prover time.
    This paper presents Chimera, a hybrid GPU backend for Spartan’s committed-Sumcheck phases. Chimera
uploads a large active polynomial state once on the GPU, keeps it resident across profitable rounds, computes
round evaluation and folding on GPU, and returns only compact round messages to Spartan’s host transcript.
Small domains and late rounds fall back to host execution when GPU overhead dominates. This boundary
preserves Spartan’s proof semantics while avoiding repeated movement of full polynomial state. Chimera also
optimizes the committed-Sumcheck wrapper around the GPU backend. Once large polynomial scans and
folds are accelerated, Spartan’s small commitments, transcript interaction, target-commitment arithmetic,
and dot-product proof construction become more visible. Chimera specializes these wrapper operations and
adds a memory-aware streaming/chunking path for when the resident state is too large for GPU memory.
    We evaluate Chimera on BN254 Spartan R1CS instances. Across a 210 –227 constraints range, Chimera
improves committed-Sumcheck region by 1.85×–17× (Fig. 1), while end-to-end proving improves for all sizes
and reaches 1.27×–1.64× speedup for 224 –227 (Table 3). We also use CUDA API orchestration measurements
to compare Chimera with the production CUDA Sumcheck backend exposed through a general library
interface of ICICLE [9]; this comparison is used to study orchestration structure.
    Overall, our work makes the following contributions:
 – We characterize the systems bottleneck in prover-integrated Sumcheck acceleration.
 – We design Chimera, a hybrid GPU-CPU backend for Spartan that keeps large polynomial state resident
   on the GPU while preserving Spartan’s transcript, proof object, and verifier semantics.
 – We implement Spartan-specific GPU support for the cubic and quadratic Sumcheck phases in Spartan’s
   R1CS prover.
 – We evaluate Chimera end-to-end inside Spartan, showing consistent committed-Sumcheck-region accel-
   eration through 227 constraints and full-prover speedups up to 1.64×.


2     Background
2.1   Zero-Knowledge Proofs
Zero-knowledge proof systems allow a prover to convince a verifier that a computation was executed correctly
without revealing private inputs. A zkSNARK prover reduces a computation to algebraic constraints over a
finite field and produces a proof that the constraints are satisfiable. In this work, we use the BN254 field,
which refers to the 254-bit finite field used by Spartan for proof arithmetic. While verification is designed
to be fast, proving requires large algebraic workloads over the constraint system. Different proof systems
expose different dominant prover kernels. Transform-heavy designs emphasize FFT/NTT and multi-scalar
multiplication (MSM), while multilinear proof systems rely more heavily on repeated evaluation and folding
of multilinear tables through Sumcheck.
    This shift changes the accelerator design problem. A kernel such as MSM or NTT can often be treated as
a large standalone batch operation. Sumcheck instead is highly parallel inside each round, but the rounds are
connected by a protocol dependency: the next round depends on the challenge produced after the current
round. Early rounds expose enough parallelism to benefit from GPU execution, but later rounds shrink
quickly and can become dominated by launch, synchronization, and CPU-GPU boundary overhead. A useful


                                                     2
backend must therefore manage memory residency, round-to-round state, transcript synchronization, and
fallback to profitable designs, rather than offloading one round kernel.

2.2   Sumcheck as a Prover Primitive
The Sumcheck protocol is a fundamental primitive for proving claims involving exponentially large sums,
i.e., sums of polynomial evaluations over the Boolean hypercube. Given a polynomial
                                                 F (x1 , . . . , xℓ )
over a finite field F, the prover wishes to convince the verifier of a claim
                                                      X
                                               S=          F (x),
                                                    x∈{0,1}ℓ

where the summation ranges over all 2ℓ Boolean assignments to the variables of F . Rather than evaluating
all 2ℓ terms of this sum directly, Sumcheck reduces this global claim through ℓ interactive rounds. In each
round r, the prover sends a univariate polynomial gr that captures the contribution of one variable, and
the verifier responds with a random challenge αr . The challenge fixes one variable, reducing the remaining
claim to a smaller instance. Repeating this process reduces the original exponential-size claim to a final point
evaluation.
    For implementation purposes, each round can be viewed as a transition over an active evaluation table:
                                            Er → gr → αr → Er+1 .
The table Er is the current list of polynomial evaluations that remain after the first r variables have been
fixed by previous challenges.
    The fold operation combines pairs of entries in Er . Consider a pair (v0 , v1 ), where v0 and v1 correspond
to setting the current variable to 0 and 1. Given the challenge αr , the folded value is
                                             v ′ = v0 + αr (v1 − v0 ).
Repeating this operation for every pair produces Er+1 , whose length is half the length of Er .
    This round structure determines the systems’ challenge addressed in this paper. A Sumcheck accelera-
tor must process large evaluation tables efficiently, reduce them to compact round messages, and update
the active state repeatedly while preserving the transcript-derived challenge sequence required for proof
correctness.

2.3   Sumcheck Inside Spartan
Spartan is a general-purpose zkSNARK for Rank-1 Constraint System (R1CS) satisfiability that does not
require a trusted setup [15]. An R1CS instance represents a computation as algebraic constraints over a
finite field, and the Spartan prover must convince the verifier that it knows a satisfying assignment to those
constraints. Spartan achieves this using multilinear-polynomial encodings and Sumcheck-based arguments.
    In Spartan, Sumcheck is embedded inside the committed proving system. The prover not only computes
round polynomials; it must also commit to round-polynomial objects, update transcript state, derive Fiat-
Shamir challenges, maintain target commitments, construct dot-product proofs, and assemble proof objects
expected by the verifier.
    The Spartan R1CS prover contains two Sumcheck phases. The first phase uses a cubic-additive relation
over polynomial evaluation tables, written in this work as
                                                  A(BC − D),
and the second phase uses a quadratic relation
                                                       AB.
Here, A, B, C, and D are phase-specific multilinear evaluation tables constructed from the R1CS instance
and witness. These relations determine the number of dense polynomial inputs, the degree of the round
message, and the layout of the folded state.


                                                          3
2.4   GPU Execution Considerations
GPU acceleration is most effective when large, regular data-parallel work can be kept on the device across
multiple operations. For Sumcheck, this means that the large active evaluation tables should remain GPU-
resident, and round evaluation and folding execute on the device. If each round separately allocates buffers,
copies full polynomials across the host-device boundary, launches small kernels, and synchronizes before the
next challenge, orchestration overhead can dominate the field arithmetic.
    This is especially important because the active Sumcheck domain shrinks by half after every round. Early
rounds expose enough parallelism to amortize GPU setup and launch overhead, but later rounds may be
faster on the CPU. A profitable backend must therefore switch execution modes as the active domain shrinks.


3     Standalone GPU Sumcheck Primitive
3.1   Motivation and Role of the Standalone Sumcheck Engine
We first study Sumcheck in isolation as a decoupled GPU primitive (i.e., standalone engine). This archi-
tectural sandbox provides a controlled environment to evaluate GPU techniques free from a full prover’s
constraints, giving us absolute control over memory layout, buffer lifetimes, folding policies, and field repre-
sentations. By testing these optimizations independently, we establish the maximum theoretical speedup of
the GPU arithmetic. The resulting high-performance kernels and memory-management strategies serve as
the direct building blocks for Chimera, which ultimately integrates these exact kernels into Spartan while
preserving its strict commitment and proof-layout requirements.

3.2   Baseline Orchestration Profiling
ICICLE implements a GPU Sumcheck primitive through an installed CUDA backend plugin. We profile
this path to quantify time spent in orchestration rather than arithmetic. Sumcheck is latency-sensitive: each
round exposes substantial data parallelism, but the protocol proceeds through a sequence of dependent
rounds. If every round introduces such overhead, the GPU may spend a significant amount of time waiting
on orchestration.
    Our ICICLE CUDA Sumcheck profile shows that this orchestration is a major part of the Sumcheck
path on GPU. In the CUDA Sumcheck trace performed using Nsight Systems, there were over a thousand
CUDA API calls during proof generation, including 435 cudaLaunchKernel calls, 639 cudaMemcpyAsync calls,
229 cudaMallocAsync calls, and 608 cudaStreamSynchronize calls. This profile motivates an execution
model that reduces repeated allocation, fragmented launches, host-device transfers, and round-boundary
synchronization.

3.3   Core GPU Optimizations
Our techniques below target the concrete overheads observed in the CUDA baseline. Our standalone engine
keeps the active state resident, reuses workspaces, folds destructively, and minimizes round-boundary host
involvement. We use product-2 to denote the quadratic relation F (A, B) = A · B over two multilinear
evaluation tables.

Persistent State and Destructive Folding. Our standalone engine removes per-round allocation from the
Sumcheck path by pre-allocating the active evaluation arrays, folded-output buffers, reduction workspace,
transcript workspace, challenge storage, and validation outputs. These buffers persist across the proof, so
each round reuses an existing execution workspace.
   The engine also uses destructive folding. After the challenge for round r is derived, the current active
table is no longer needed in its original form; the protocol only requires the folded table for round r + 1. The
engine therefore uses a ping-pong layout, consuming one buffer and writing the folded state into the other.
This optimization is primarily about memory capacity rather than latency.


                                                       4
CUDA Graph Scheduling. For a fixed active-table size, our standalone Sumcheck loop has a fixed sequence
of CUDA kernels. The engine therefore captures this sequence as a CUDA Graph and replays it across
repeated proofs. This reduces launch scheduling overhead, but only modestly after persistent buffers are
already in place: relative to the persistent-buffer path without graph replay, CUDA Graphs provide only a
small additional gain after most per-proof setup cost has already been removed.

Round-Message Reduction. Each Sumcheck round reduces a large active evaluation table into a constant-size
round message. For the product-2 relation, the round message contains only three field elements. Notably,
this creates a critical-path reduction: all block-local contributions must be accumulated before the transcript
can absorb the round message and derive the next challenge. If the large table scan is parallel, but the final
round-message aggregation is serial, the reduction becomes a significant bottleneck.
    The optimized reduction parallelizes aggregation across the block partials for each round-polynomial
coefficient. The final constant-size message is therefore assembled using block level parallelism to avoid
serializing the critical path.

Fused Fold-and-Build. After the challenge αr is known, the prover folds the active table and then constructs
the next round message. A direct implementation performs these as two separate passes: first fold and write
the next active table, then read that folded table again to build the next round polynomial. This schedule is
correct but consumes excessive memory bandwidth and introduces latency.
    Our standalone engine fuses these two steps. Once αr is available, the engine folds the current state and
immediately uses the folded values to begin constructing the next round message. This optimization does
not change the protocol: the fold still happens only after the challenge is known, and the next round message
is still computed from the correctly folded state. Thus, this avoids a full traversal of the folded table.

Montgomery Resident Sumcheck State. The Sumcheck protocol works over the BN254 scalar field, whose
operations are performed modulo a large prime p. Every multiplication of two field elements produces a
large intermediate value that must be reduced modulo p. This modular reduction is expensive on GPU:
it involves multi-limb arithmetic, carry propagation, and conditional subtraction. Repeated conversion be-
tween canonical and arithmetic representations would add a full-state cost at every round. To avoid this,
our standalone Sumcheck uses Montgomery arithmetic. Field elements are converted into the Montgomery
domain when they enter the GPU workspace. Multiplication is performed by Montgomery reduction, which
uses word-level multiply-adds, shifts, carry propagation and correction steps that are more suited to fixed
limb GPU arithmetic.
    Our standalone engine therefore converts the active evaluation arrays into Montgomery form once before
the round loop. Round evaluation, accumulation, reduction, and folding operate on Montgomery values and
the folded state remains in Montgomery for the next round to consume directly.

GPU Transcript and Challenge Generation. Our standalone engine keeps transcript construction and chal-
lenge generation on the GPU. The compact round message is canonicalized for the transcript, the transcript
input bytes are built on device, Keccak is computed on device, and the digest is reduced to a BN254 chal-
lenge on device. The resulting challenge is then consumed directly by the fold step. This produces a fully
device-side round transition in our engine.

Out-of-Core Chunking, Hybrid Tail and Pipelining. Full GPU residency is the preferred execution mode
when the active state fits in device memory, but large instances can exceed available VRAM. Our standalone
engine adds a chunked mode which streams chunks of the evaluation table through bounded GPU memory
instead of placing the full active state on device. Each chunk contributes to the round message and is folded
into the next active representation. Chunking is a scalability mechanism, not the fastest path when resident
execution fits. For a 220 -entry product-2 instance, the resident working-set estimate is 0.0939 GiB, while the
chunk buffer is 0.015625 GiB, which corresponds to a 6.0× reduction.
    The chunked path also uses pipelining to overlap chunk transfers with GPU computation. Relative to the
non-pipelined chunked path, pipelining improves the 220 -entry chunked case from 41.47 ms to 14.66 ms. The

3.4    Standalone Component Performance Evaluation

Table 1 summarizes the retained standalone product-2 Sumcheck components. The resident speed rows use
the fixed-size N = 222 instance and report each runtime relative to the comparison point shown in the table.
The chunked rows are reported separately because they measure the bounded-memory execution path rather
than the resident path.
   The resident path improves from 62.911 ms to 28.552 ms, an overall 2.20× speedup. When compared
against an external baseline in the same standalone N = 222 product-2 timing harness, the optimized path
takes 28.7 ms versus 84.2 ms for ICICLE CUDA, a 2.94× speedup. Chunked execution is reported separately
because it targets memory capacity.


3.5    Implications for Transitioning to Spartan Integration

Our standalone engine identifies GPU Sumcheck techniques, but cannot be inserted into Spartan unchanged.
Spartan must preserve transcript semantics, proof layout, commitment interfaces, and host-side R1CS data
structures. These requirements make some host-visible boundaries necessary. Chimera, our Sumcheck back-
end for Spartan, uses a prover-compatible CPU-GPU hybrid design. GPU kernels accelerate large round
evaluation and folding, there is resident storage for large active arrays, Montgomery arithmetic inside the
kernels, phase-level GPU-side state construction, and CPU fallback for small domains. At the same time,
Spartan remains responsible for the transcript and commitments. In each round, the GPU produces the
compact round message, Spartan derives the challenge, and the challenge is returned to the GPU for folding.
    Thus, Chimera is neither a standalone engine embedded directly into Spartan nor a call to a generic
CUDA Sumcheck primitive. It is a judicious integration that adopts profitable primitive-level techniques
while balancing GPU throughput, host transcript compatibility, setup cost, commitment overhead, and
small-round overhead.


4     Chimera: Hybrid Sumcheck Backend for Spartan

The standalone engine identifies useful primitive-level GPU techniques. Chimera adapts those techniques to
Spartan’s committed-Sumcheck prover while preserving the transcript, commitment interface, proof objects,
and verifier behavior.


                                                             6
4.1   Design Goal and Integration Boundary

Chimera’s goal is to accelerate Spartan’s committed-Sumcheck phases without changing the proof interface.
The backend therefore accelerates the full phase execution path (round evaluation, folding, boundary trans-
fer, and the surrounding committed-Sumcheck work) while preserving the transcript order, commitment
behavior, proof-object layout, and verifier behavior expected by Spartan.
    Chimera uses a phase-level backend boundary. At the start of each Sumcheck phase, Spartan transfers
the active evaluation buffers to the GPU. Across the phase, the GPU keeps this state resident, computes each
round message, and folds the active arrays after receiving Spartan’s challenge. Only compact data crosses the
boundary: round messages, Fiat-Shamir challenges, and final claims. This preserves Spartan’s proof-facing
structure while avoiding repeated data movement.
    This boundary avoids two unattractive extremes. A per-round or per-kernel GPU interface would repeat-
edly move the Sumcheck polynomial state and pay coordination overhead at every round. A fully device-
owned Sumcheck path would conflict with Spartan’s host-visible transcript, round-polynomial commitments,
and committed-Sumcheck proof objects. The GPU is also not always the fastest choice for every part of a
round or for every round of committed-Sumcheck. As the active domain shrinks, late rounds expose less
parallelism and can become dominated by launch, synchronization, and boundary overhead. In those cases,
native Spartan execution may be faster.
    Thus, Chimera targets useful GPU residency rather than maximum GPU ownership. It uses the GPU
when the active polynomial state is large enough to amortize boundary cost, preserves Spartan ownership
where proof semantics require it, and optimizes the committed-Sumcheck wrapper once polynomial evaluation
and folding no longer dominate runtime.


4.2   Kernel and Wrapper Optimizations

Chimera accelerates the two Sumcheck phases used by Spartan’s R1CS prover. The first phase uses the
cubic-additive relation A(BC − D), while the second phase uses the quadratic relation AB. These relations
determine the degree of the round polynomial, the number of values returned to Spartan, and the layout of
the folded state. Chimera also optimizes the committed-Sumcheck wrapper that connects those rounds to
Spartan’s proof interface.

Round-kernel acceleration. The GPU kernels accelerate the large round evaluation and folding work directly.
In the measured Spartan setting, quadratic round-and-fold kernels are 8.45–10.38× faster than the baseline
Spartan path, while cubic kernels are 2.02× faster. The lower cubic speedup reflects the heavier relation and
additional input state.

Resident phase state. A per-round GPU kernel call still pays repeated setup and movement of large mul-
tilinear evaluation tables. Chimera instead keeps the active phase polynomials resident on the GPU across
rounds: the active polynomial buffers are uploaded once, round messages are computed from resident state,
and folds are applied on device after Spartan returns the transcript challenge. Only compact protocol values
(i.e., round messages, challenges, and final claims) cross the CPU-GPU boundary.

Native-fallback for small domains. GPU residency is not profitable for every Sumcheck round. As folding
halves the active domain, late rounds expose little parallelism. At those sizes, GPU launch, synchronization,
and host-device boundary overheads can dominate the saved arithmetic. Chimera therefore keeps large active
domains on the resident GPU path but falls back to optimized CPU code for small late-round domains.

Committed-wrapper specialization. After round evaluation and folding are accelerated, Spartan’s committed-
Sumcheck wrapper becomes a dominant local cost. The wrapper includes small round-polynomial commit-
ments, target-commitment arithmetic, transcript interaction, and dot-product proof construction. Chimera
therefore optimizes the committed-Sumcheck pipeline around the GPU engine. Spartan’s round polynomials
are degree two in the quadratic phase and degree three in the cubic phase, so using a general MSM style path

preserving transcript order and proof-object structure.

Memory-aware chunking. Full residency is fastest when the active polynomial state fits in GPU memory,
but it does not scale indefinitely. Chunking is the bounded-memory path: instead of materializing the full
phase-two quadratic state at once, Chimera streams slices of the active domain through GPU memory and
reduces each slice into the same compact round-message values expected by Spartan.
    At N = 216 , the phase-two quadratic active evaluation table length is n = 131072. A full resident evaluator
stores two dense polynomials, requiring 2 · 131072 · 32 = 8.0 MiB for 32-byte BN254 field elements. With
chunk pairs = 8192, the chunked evaluator stores only the current low/high slices of both polynomials,
requiring 4 · 8192 · 32 = 1.0 MiB. This gives an 8.0× smaller working set. We report this as a memory-
scaling result rather than a latency speedup because the integrated path prioritizes bounded memory over
the pipelined latency optimizations used in the standalone engine.

Fused phase-2 evaluation-table construction. Before the second Sumcheck begins, Spartan constructs the
phase-2 polynomial used by the quadratic relation. The original path built three dense evaluation tables for
A(rx, ·), B(rx, ·), and C(rx, ·), and then made a second pass to combine them into rA A(rx, ·) + rB B(rx, ·) +
rC C(rx, ·).
   Chimera removes that extra materialization step. Instead of building three temporary dense tables and
then combining them, it accumulates the weighted sparse contributions directly into the final phase-2 eval-
uation table.

4.3   Ablation Study
Table 2 attributes Chimera’s committed-Sumcheck speedup to the main optimizations in the final system
(evaluated at N = 217 ). Each row reports what the optimization does, its attributed acceleration factor,
and its share of the overall committed-Sumcheck acceleration. Overall, these factors multiply to about 7.96×
speedup from clean Spartan to Chimera.
   The optimizations are dependent, so their effects overlap. The main example is the committed-Sumcheck
path. GPU-resident kernels make round evaluation and folding fast, but the original CPU committed-proof
path can still surround and delay those GPU rounds through tiny commitments, comm target MSMs, re-
dundant commitment work, and small DotProductProofs. Chimera’s committed-Sumcheck GPU integration
removes this serial CPU path, allowing the GPU-backed Sumcheck engine to determine the region time.
Hybrid scheduling avoids inefficient GPU tail rounds, and the phase-2 feed path prepares the quadratic
Sumcheck input directly for GPU-backed execution.
   Some of these optimizations remove fixed or weakly scaling committed-proof overheads around the GPU
backend, while others accelerate the large polynomial scan-and-fold work. As N grows, the region contains

5     Experimental Evaluation

We evaluate Chimera as a Spartan-compatible backend for committed-Sumcheck using BN254 R1CS in-
stances with equal number of constraints and variables on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 with 32 GB of
memory over PCIe Gen5 x16, driver 591.86, and CUDA 13.1. The main metrics are end-to-end Spartan
prover speedup, committed-Sumcheck-region speedup and CUDA orchestration activity. GPU timings ex-
clude CUDA context initialization and use warmed-up runs, because prover services amortize initialization
across many proofs.
    The baseline is the original Spartan prover running on CPU. This is the appropriate comparison because
Spartan does not provide an upstream GPU backend for committed-Sumcheck. Therefore, our evaluation
measures the end-to-end effect of adding Chimera to Spartan, rather than comparing against a nonexistent
GPU implementation.
    The committed-Sumcheck region includes the work required to execute Spartan’s two Sumcheck phases
inside the prover, including phase setup, round-message computation, folding, transcript interaction, small
round-polynomial commitments, target updates, and proof-wrapper work. This region is broader than a
standalone Sumcheck kernel timing, so it captures the integration costs that appear when Sumcheck is
embedded in a committed proof system.


5.1   Spartan End-to-End Performance

All Spartan experiments use the BN254 scalar field and synthetic R1CS instances with equal numbers of
constraints and variables. Chimera preserves Spartan’s proof interface: the cryptographic transcript, proof
objects, commitments, and verifier behavior are unchanged. The backend is selected at the Sumcheck phase-
level. Small active domains run on the CPU path, while large domains use the resident GPU backend; the
switch is automatic.
    Table 3 shows complete Spartan prover time from 212 through 227 constraints. Chimera improves end-
to-end prover time across all measured sizes, with speedups ranging from 1.03× to 1.64×. The gains are
modest at small and mid-sized instances because full prover time includes work outside Chimera’s target
region, including witness processing, polynomial commitment, phase preparation, transcript setup, and proof
assembly. As the instance size grows, the accelerated committed-Sumcheck region becomes a larger part of
the prover, and Chimera reaches 1.27×–1.64× end-to-end speedup for N = 224 –227 .
    Figure 1 isolates the committed-Sumcheck region. Chimera is faster across the full measured range, but
the region speedup narrows as N grows. This is because the measured region is not only round evaluation
and folding. It also includes phase setup, phase-2 table construction, transcript interaction, small round-
polynomial commitments, target updates, dot-product proof work, backend selection, and late rounds whose
active domains are too small to efficiently occupy the GPU. Once large scans and folds are accelerated, these
fixed and less-parallel costs become visible.

5.2   CUDA Orchestration Comparison

We also compare Chimera’s execution model with ICICLE’s CUDA Sumcheck backend. The controlled
ICICLE trace uses standalone inputs matching Spartan’s two Sumcheck phase sizes, while Chimera uses
the corresponding Spartan-integrated phases. The comparison therefore fixes the Sumcheck scale and round
count; the remaining difference is the backend boundary. Recall from Section 3.4 that our optimized execution
model achieves a 2.94× raw speedup over this ICICLE baseline.
    Figure 2 shows that Chimera performs fewer host-visible CUDA API operations in the profiled run.
ICICLE exposes Sumcheck through a general backend boundary, so allocation, copies, launches, and syn-
chronization are managed behind the library interface. Chimera instead exposes phase-resident state directly
to Spartan: state new uploads active arrays once, round evals computes compact round messages from
resident buffers, fold updates the resident state after Spartan returns the challenge, and final claims are
copied back at the end of the phase.


5.3   Discussion

The results show that prover-integrated Sumcheck acceleration is not only a kernel optimization problem.
Once large round evaluation and folding are faster, fixed and less-parallel costs become visible: setup, tran-
script interaction, small commitments, target updates, dot-product proof work, backend selection, and mem-
ory movement.
    These results also show why backend phase boundary matters. A fine-grained GPU interface repeatedly
pays transfer, launch, and synchronization costs, while a fully device-owned path would duplicate Spartan’s
transcript and proof-object logic. Chimera uses an intermediate boundary: the GPU owns large resident
polynomial state, while Spartan owns the proof-facing protocol state.
    The next bottlenecks are therefore outside the resident round kernels: larger polynomial commitment
paths, remaining proof-wrapper costs, and a complete streaming backend with chunked folding and double-
buffered transfers.


6     Related Work

Prior ZKP acceleration systems target prover bottlenecks such as MSM, NTT/FFT, polynomial computa-
tion, batching, and pipelined proof generation [2–4, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 21]. These systems show that prover

performance depends on arithmetic throughput, memory movement, scheduling, and hardware/software co-
design. Chimera is complementary: it targets committed-Sumcheck inside Spartan, where the bottleneck is
a sequence of transcript-dependent rounds over shrinking multilinear tables.
    Cryptographic GPU libraries such as ICICLE expose reusable CUDA backends for finite-field and proof-
system primitives [9]. This production model is useful, but a general library boundary can hide memory
lifetime, allocation, synchronization, and round scheduling decisions. Chimera instead exposes a resident
Sumcheck state to Spartan so that active polynomial buffers remain live across rounds.
    Spartan and related multilinear proof systems use Sumcheck as a central prover primitive [1, 15, 19, 20].
In these systems, Sumcheck is not an isolated kernel: each round is wrapped by transcript updates, commit-
ments, target-commitment updates, and proof-object construction. Chimera addresses this integration gap
by accelerating the large round-evaluation and folding work while preserving Spartan’s transcript, commit-
ments, and verifier semantics.


7   Conclusion

This paper presented Chimera, a Spartan-compatible GPU backend for accelerating committed-Sumcheck.
Chimera keeps large polynomial state resident on the GPU, executes round evaluation and folding on device,
returns only compact protocol values to Spartan, and falls back to native execution when late-round domains
are too small for profitable GPU use. This boundary preserves Spartan’s transcript, commitment behavior,
proof objects, and verifier compatibility.
    On BN254 Spartan R1CS instances, Chimera achieves a speedup of 7.96× in the committed-Sumcheck
region at N = 217 and improves full prover time at every measured size. End-to-end speedups range from
1.27×–1.64× for N = 224 –227 . The results show that effective prover acceleration requires more than GPU
kernels alone: Chimera’s gains come from combining GPU-resident Sumcheck execution with protocol-aware
integration, hybrid scheduling, and phase-specific dataflow.
    More broadly, Chimera shows that accelerating Sumcheck inside a prover is not only a kernel optimization
problem. The accelerator must be placed at a protocol boundary that preserves transcript and proof com-
patibility while managing resident state, host-device movement, shrinking round sizes, and committed-proof
